“VIOLENT STORM OVERWHELMED VESSEL: AIR FORCE EOD JUMPMASTER SAVES DROWNING SURVIVORS AT SEA.”

When a violent ocean storm hit with mountainous swells, freezing temperatures, and treacherous rip currents, people were thrown into the open sea and within minutes of drowning. Senior Master Sergeant Joseph Riemer dove straight in.

An elite Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) flight leader and the first EOD technician in U.S. Air Force history to earn the Military Freefall Jumpmaster Badge, Riemer was at sea when disaster struck:

Hearing desperate cries for help, Riemer immediately plunged into the freezing, turbulent ocean, battling massive swells and rip currents to reach the scattered victims.

Reaching the survivors, Riemer used water survival techniques to keep them afloat, quickly assessing that two airmen had exhausted their strength and were moments away from slipping beneath the surface.

Fighting Back with Flotation Gear: Riemer fought his way back through the punishing waves to the boat, retrieved emergency life preservers, swam back into the violent sea, and secured the drowning victims in flotation vests.

 Swimming against powerful currents, he towed the victims through the swells to within 25 meters of the vessel, secured a heavy safety line, and hauled them safely aboard before ensuring everyone was accounted for on the return to port.

In March 2025, Brigadier General Brian Hartless presented Senior Master Sergeant Joseph Riemer with the Airman’s Medal—the Department of the Air Force's highest decoration for heroism outside of combat.

A combat veteran of Operations Enduring Freedom, Inherent Resolve, and Freedom's Sentinel, Riemer currently serves as the Senior Enlisted Leader for the Air Force Civil Engineer Center EOD Division at Tyndall Air Force Base, where he was also named the 2024 AFMC Outstanding EOD Master Blaster of the Year.

Trump just noticed the gas price drop… and questioned the timing.

Gas prices have fallen sharply.
According to AAA, the national average is now around $3.75 a gallon — down roughly 55 cents in the past month.

Trump’s response?
“Notice that they waited until after the ‘election?’”

He offered no evidence that the drop was deliberately delayed.
In reality, prices had already been trending downward in the weeks leading up to Election Day, driven by normal seasonal factors, higher production, and lower demand.

Still, the comment landed exactly as intended.
When prices are high, politicians get blamed.
When they fall, the same politicians often claim credit — or in this case, raise suspicions about the timing.

Whether you see it as a fair question or classic political deflection, one thing is clear:
Gas prices remain one of the most emotionally charged numbers in American politics.

What do you make of the timing claim?

What started as a late-night food run turned into a lifesaving rescue when three U.S. Marines stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort pulled an unconscious driver from a burning pickup truck on Parris Island Gateway.

The Beaufort County Sheriff's Office honored Cpl. Nathan C. Armstrong, Cpl. Isaac T. Ames, and Cpl. Caleb L. Crawford—alongside a responding sheriff's deputy—with Life Saving Awards and medals for their actions during the Aug. 3 fiery crash.

Semper Fi to these three Marines—drop a salute in the comments.

#USMC #Marines #SemperFi

The duct-taped American Airlines passenger just had his state charges dropped.

You remember the video.
A passenger completely wrapped in duct tape and zip ties, restrained in his seat after an alleged mid-flight meltdown.

On a September 3 American Airlines flight from Dallas to Newark, Arthur “Layne” Lundeen is accused of launching into racial slurs, anti-gay insults, and disruptive behavior toward the crew.
Fellow passengers eventually taped him down.
The flight was forced to divert to Baltimore.

Maryland had charged him with second-degree assault and disorderly conduct.
Those state charges have now been dropped.

Prosecutors say the incident happened in the air, so it falls under federal jurisdiction.
He still faces federal charges for interfering with the flight crew.

The viral video made the story famous.
The legal outcome is turning out more complicated than a lot of people expected.

What do you think about the charges being dropped at the state level?

FORT BENNING, Ga. (APRIL 24, 2013) -- The family of Sgt. 1st Class Kenneth Westbrook was presented with his Silver Star for gallantry, and his second Combat Infantryman Badge, April 19, during an emotional ceremony at Derby Auditorium here.

Westbrook died Oct. 7, 2009, as a result of wounds suffered Sept. 8, 2009, when insurgents attacked his unit in the Ganjgal Valley, Afghanistan.

With the award coming nearly three and a half years after his death, Westbrook's wife, Charlene, said she felt an immense sense of pride in her husband.

"I would say that I'm so very proud of him and that he's my hero," she said. "Actually, he'd probably grimace and say, 'No, I'm not a hero. I'm just doing my job.'"

The Silver Star is the Army's third highest award for gallantry, behind only the Distinguished Service Cross and the Medal of Honor.

“End of an era.”
The Navy is discontinuing the peacoat after more than a century. 

That heavy, double-breasted wool coat has been part of the Navy’s look for generations.
Starting October 1, 2027, it will no longer be authorized.

The same goes for the officer reefer coat.
Both are being replaced by a modern synthetic parka.

The change is part of a larger effort to lighten the seabag and simplify what sailors have to carry and maintain.
Navy message NAVADMIN 270/26 lays it out clearly.

For a lot of people who served, the peacoat wasn’t just a coat.
It was the thing you put on when the weather got nasty, the one that showed up in photos, the one that felt like the Navy.

Now it’s being phased out for something lighter, more practical, and easier to maintain.

Tradition versus efficiency.
Another small piece of the old Navy is moving into history.

How do you feel about losing the peacoat?

Sfc. Hester is one of the few women to be awarded for valor in close-quarters combat.

Leigh Ann Hester was a sergeant with the National Guard’s Kentucky-based 617th Military Police Company when she was deployed to Iraq, and in 2005, she was scanning and clearing a route for a supply convoy near Baghdad when her squad was ambushed by enemy fire.

She was trained for this, as it was a risk that came with her daily job in Iraq. Thus, when they became under attack, she knew exactly what to do. She directed her team away from the enemy’s intense fire and into a flanking position that exposed multiple irrigation ditches and an orchard that the enemies were using to stage the attack.

She was initially directing fire, then began fighting on foot. Sgt. Hester displayed incredible bravery as she had walked directly into the line of fire to kill at least three enemy combatants at close range, resulting in numerous convoy members lives saved. With thirty-three insurgents killed or wounded and one captured, every member of her unit survived.

Her heroic actions led her to become the first woman since World War II to earn the Silver Star Medal and the very first to ever earn it for combat valor.
Sgt. Hester separated from the National Guard and became a police officer after she returned to the United States; a job she had wanted since childhood. But she enjoyed being a soldier so much so, that she rejoined the National Guard shortly after.

In 2014, she spent 18 months in Afghanistan, where she was promoted to sergeant first class. And in 2017, she was sent to the Virgin Islands as part of the international humanitarian effort in the wake of Hurricane Maria.

U.S. Army V Corps just rolled out a sweeping update to its rules for soldiers in Poland and 15 other European nations — and the list is specific.

Under the Nov. 5 order signed by V Corps commander Lt. Gen. Thomas Feltey, troops are barred from visiting bars, strip clubs, nightclubs, karaoke spots, and hookah lounges. Soldiers are also prohibited from "approaching, handling, feeding, capturing, adopting, harassing, disturbing, or otherwise interfering with wildlife," buying vapes from unauthorized vendors, or leaving base between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. without a battle buddy.

V Corps says the move isn't tied to a single spike in misconduct, but is meant to preserve "good order, discipline, and the safety of our personnel" so units stay ready to "Fight Tonight."

The Marine Corps abruptly relieved Col. Eric Meador from command of the Tactical Training Exercise Control Group at Twentynine Palms on Nov. 9 without giving a reason.

A Marine Corps spokesperson confirmed the dismissal Sunday, citing the "administrative nature of this action" for withholding details, and Meador's biography was scrubbed from the training unit's website. Meador, who joined the Corps in 1991 and has led the combined-arms training group since August 2025, previously deployed to Iraq, Afghanistan, and Djibouti and earned a Bronze Star with combat distinguishing device and two Combat Action Ribbons.

Should the military be required to disclose why senior commanders are relieved?

The Air Force just trained 1,518 new pilots in one year — the most since 1991.

For years the pilot shortage has been one of the biggest quiet crises in the U.S. military.
At one point the Air Force was roughly 2,400 pilots short of what it needed.

That number just took a real hit.

In fiscal 2026 the service graduated 1,518 new pilots — the highest total in 35 years.
The last time they hit numbers like this was 1991.

A big reason for the jump?
They moved a large portion of early flight training over to civilian flight schools.
More capacity. Faster pipeline. Same standards.

It’s not a complete fix yet.
Retention and experience levels still matter.
But for the first time in a long time, the production side is finally catching up.

Some will say this is the beginning of the end of the shortage.
Others will wait to see if the Air Force can keep this pace year after year.

Either way… 1,518 new pilots is a serious step in the right direction.

Is the shortage finally over?

Iran aimed drones at U.S. forces again.
U.S. jets just hit back. 

For the third time in a week, Iranian drones targeted American personnel and assets in Bahrain.

This time the U.S. response came fast.

On November 17, American fighter jets struck an IRGC missile launch site on Iran’s Qeshm Island using precision munitions.
The Pentagon is calling it self-defense.

No U.S. casualties reported from the latest drone attack.
Iranian officials claim the strike on Qeshm caused no major damage to civilian areas.

This is the same pattern we’ve seen for months:
Iran probes with drones.
The U.S. answers with limited, targeted strikes.

Some say these measured responses are the right way to avoid a wider war.
Others argue that after multiple attacks, a stronger message is needed.

The question now is simple:

Strong enough response?

House Democrats officially nominated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York on Wednesday to be Speaker of the House, positioning him to become the first Black speaker in U.S. history when the 120th Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027.

Jeffries ran unopposed in the Democratic caucus alongside Rep. Katherine Clark for majority leader and Rep. Pete Aguilar for majority whip. Supporters point to his coalition-building and focus on lowering costs and oversight, while some progressive voices have urged a more aggressive approach and House Republicans have nominated Rep. Jim Jordan to oppose the Democratic agenda.

Do you support this move, and what should the top priority be for the next Congress?

74 years ago today, one American pilot took on seven Soviet MiGs… alone. 

November 18, 1952.
Navy Lieutenant Royce Williams was flying an F9F Panther off the coast of Korea when he suddenly found himself facing seven Soviet MiG-15s.

Outnumbered.
Outmatched in speed and climb.
And completely alone.

For 35 minutes — the longest dogfight in U.S. Navy history — Williams fought them.
He shot down four of the Soviet jets.
His plane was hit by a 37mm cannon shell, hydraulics failing, yet he still made it back to the carrier and landed.

Because the enemy pilots were Soviet (not North Korean or Chinese), the entire engagement was classified.
Williams was ordered to keep quiet.
He did — for more than 50 years.

Only after the Cold War ended did the full story come out.
In February of this year, at age 100, he finally received the Medal of Honor.
He is now 101.

One man.
Seven enemy jets.
Four confirmed kills.
And a secret kept for half a century.

Some stories still stop you cold.

Nine years in a row, and the Pentagon still hasn't passed an audit.

The Defense Department just failed its fiscal 2026 financial audit covering $4.9 trillion in assets and $5.2 trillion in liabilities across 149 separate financial systems — some still running on 50-year-old code.

Officials say 14 of 25 standalone entities passed this year, up from 11 last year, and they're now using Palantir and xAI tools to try to reach a clean audit by 2028.

If an everyday American failed an IRS audit nine times in a row, what would happen?

Matthew Gene "Axe" Axelson (June 25, 1976 – June 28, 2005) was a United States Navy SEAL who was killed in the War in Afghanistan. He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions and valor during Operation Red Wings, in which he was killed. He served in that operation along with Michael Murphy, Daniel Dietz, and Marcus Luttrell. Dietz and Luttrell were also awarded the Navy Cross, the Purple Heart, and the Navy good conduct medals, where Murphy received the Medal of Honor.

Citation: For extraordinary heroism in actions against the enemy while serving in a four-man Special Reconnaissance element with SEAL Delivery Vehicle Team ONE, Naval Special Warfare Task unit, Afghanistan from 27 to 28 June 2005. Petty Officer Axelson demonstrated extraordinary heroism in the face of grave danger in the vicinity of Asadabad, Konar Province, Afghanistan. Operating in the middle of an enemy-controlled area, in extremely rugged terrain, his Special Reconnaissance element was tasked with locating a high-level Anti-Coalition Militia leader, in support of a follow-on direct action mission to disrupt enemy activity. On 28 June 2005, the element was spotted by Anti-Coalition Militia sympathizers, who immediately revealed their position to the militia fighters. As a result, the element directly encountered the enemy. Demonstrating exceptional resolve and fully understanding the gravity of the situation, Petty Officer Axelson's element bravely engaged the militia, who held both a numerical and positional advantage. The ensuing firefight resulted in numerous enemy personnel killed, with several of the Navy members suffering casualties. Ignoring his injuries and demonstrating exceptional composure, Petty Officer Axelson advised the teammate closest to him to escape while he provided cover fire. With total disregard for his own life and thinking only of his teammate's survival, he continued to attack the enemy, eliminating additional militia fighters, until he was mortally wounded by enemy fire. A champion of freedom, Petty Officer Axelson will be remembered for his self-sacrificing actions in the continuing Global War on Terrorism. By his undaunted courage, fortitude under fire, and unwavering dedication to duty, Petty Officer Axelson reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service. He gallantly gave his life for the cause of freedom.

TRUMP SAYS HE’LL MOVE TO ISRAEL & BECOME PRIME MINISTER IF AMERICANS “EVER GROW TIRED OF ME”

During an appearance on Fox News’ Fox & Friends, President Donald Trump delivered a viral one-liner that quickly lit up social media, quipping about a theoretical second political career across the Atlantic, as reported by The Jerusalem Post and Ticker News:

"If people ever got tired of me in the US, I'll move to Israel and become prime minister."

The remark came amid a wide-ranging discussion touching on U.S.–Israel relations, his historic diplomatic legacy in the Middle East, and his announcement of an agreed-upon plan with Benjamin Netanyahu to phase out America’s $4 billion in annual military aid subsidies by the end of the year.

The Context Behind the Viral Quip
While delivered in Trump's trademark rally style, the comment taps into a unique political dynamic between Washington and Jerusalem:

Enduring Popularity in Israel: Polling consistently shows Trump enjoying substantial approval ratings among the Israeli electorate, fueled by milestone diplomatic actions including moving the U.S. Embassy to Jerusalem, recognizing sovereignty over the Golan Heights, and brokering the landmark Abraham Accords.

Classic Media Banter: Political commentators and supporters characterized the quip as vintage Trump banter—poking fun at his domestic critics while asserting his global brand recognition and perceived standing abroad.

Bilateral Scrutiny: Critics seized on the remark to highlight the complex political relationship between Trump and Israeli right-wing leadership, debating the optics of floating foreign governance amid high-stakes domestic midterms.

“144 VESSELS REDIRECTED.” — U.S. Central Command Tightens Grip on the Strait of Hormuz Amid High-Stakes Iran Talks.

Amid ongoing diplomatic negotiations between the United States and Iran regarding security and administration across the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed that coalition and U.S. naval forces have now intercepted and redirected 144 commercial vessels under the renewed maritime blockade of traffic to and from Iranian ports.

The maritime enforcement surge comes at a pivotal diplomatic juncture:

• The Chokepoint at Stake: The Strait of Hormuz remains the world's most critical maritime energy corridor, handling roughly 20% of global petroleum transit. Control and administration of these shipping lanes remain the central sticking point in ongoing U.S.-Iran discussions.

• Enforcing the Blockade: U.S. Navy carrier strike groups, guided-missile destroyers, and maritime patrol aircraft have maintained continuous overwatch, conducting visit-board-search-and-seizure (VBSS) operations and turning back non-compliant vessels and illicit "shadow fleet" tankers attempting to evade sanctions.

• Diplomatic Leverage: By cutting off commercial cargo and petroleum shipping routes to Iranian ports, Washington is applying maximum operational pressure on Tehran while negotiating maritime protocols and regional de-escalation terms.

With 144 vessels already turned away, will this intensified carrier-backed blockade force a breakthrough at the negotiating table, or increase the risk of armed skirmishes in the Gulf?

“12,000 FEET UP A FROZEN MOUNTAIN: HE CARRIED HIS PARALYZED TEAMMATE DOWN TO AN IMPROVISED LZ.”

High-altitude mountain rescue leaves zero room for error. When a catastrophic fall in the Colorado backcountry left a Green Beret paralyzed and freezing, Sergeant First Class Bobby Haran stabilized the traumatic injuries, rigged a descent system, and hauled his teammate down a sheer rock face to an area where a rescue chopper could touch its skids.

At the summit of the 14,023-foot Wilson Peak near Telluride, Colorado, SFC Robert "Bobby" Haran an elite mountain instructor with the Special Operations Mountain Warfare Training Center (10th Special Forces Group) watched his teammate’s lead ski strike a submerged rock, releasing the binding and triggering an uncontrolled, 2,000-foot plunge down an icy couloir.

What followed was one of the most remarkable acts of alpine mountaineering and survival in Special Operations history:

Knowing that skiing the steep route solo risked triggering massive avalanches onto his injured partner, Haran descended 2,200 vertical feet on foot across near-vertical ice using only crampons and an ice axe, hauling his teammate's recovered skis to use as an emergency litter.

Reaching his teammate, Haran found him suffering from a fractured sternum, broken hip, shattered shoulder, compound leg fractures, internal bleeding, a torn aorta, and severe hypothermia. Haran stabilized his breathing and wounds in sub-zero winds.

Communicating via emergency satellite with San Miguel County Search and Rescue, Haran rigged a lowering system and moved his paralyzed teammate hundreds of feet further down sheer rock to an improvised alpine landing zone.

After a rescue helicopter hoisted the casualty to St. Mary's Hospital in Grand Junction, Haran skied the remaining backcountry miles solo back to the trailhead.

During a formal ceremony at Fort Carson, Major General Lawrence G. Ferguson presented the Soldier's Medal—the Army's highest peacetime decoration for heroism—to honor Haran's extraordinary valor and skill.

“Bobby, without a doubt, is the only individual that comes to mind that could have performed the way he did that day,” Haran’s NCOIC concluded. “Because of all his training, perseverance, and wherewithal, it resulted in him saving his teammate's life.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to become the next Chief of Staff of the Army.

LaNeve has been serving as acting Chief of Staff since Hegseth removed Gen. Randy George from the job back in April.

Before that, LaNeve served as one of Hegseth’s military aides — making this a promotion of someone the Secretary already knows and trusts.

The nomination was sent to the Senate on November 17 and still needs confirmation.

This is another major leadership move inside the Army under Hegseth’s watch.

Some will see it as putting a proven insider in charge to continue reforms.
Others will question whether promoting a former aide is the right call for the Army’s top uniformed job.

Either way, the man who has been running the Army for the past seven months is now formally in line to keep the job.

What do you think?

“PUT ELON MUSK UNDER OATH.” — GOP Lawmaker Calls for Formal Congressional Probe.

In a rare move from within his own party, Republican U.S. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania announced he is prepared to subpoena Elon Musk and place him under federal oath regarding his defense influence and reported operational restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine:

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill are increasingly scrutinizing the immense leverage single private tech executives hold over Pentagon communications, military satellite networks, and active conflict zones.

The proposed oversight probe centers on reports surrounding Starlink network connectivity during Ukrainian naval drone operations in the Black Sea and questions over security clearance standards for commercial defense contractors.

Supporters and defense analysts emphasize that SpaceX provided vital battlefield communications when legacy defense contractors failed to deliver, arguing that private enterprise shouldn't be penalized or micromanaged by politicians for preventing unauthorized geopolitical escalation.

Should Congress haul Elon Musk under federal oath to investigate private tech influence over military operations—or is this an unwarranted government attack on private innovation?

BREAKING: Sirens just went off at US bases in Kuwait.

Kuwait’s military says it is currently countering hostile drones.
Air raid sirens are sounding across parts of the country.

This comes shortly after the United States carried out a strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island.

According to Iranian media and Kuwait’s own military statements, the drones are being intercepted.
The US has not confirmed any attack on Kuwait itself.

American officials say the Qeshm strike was carried out in self-defense after Iranian drones targeted Bahrain.

Tensions in the region are rising fast.
Bases that have been relatively quiet for months are suddenly hearing sirens again.

Whether this stays limited or escalates further is still unclear.

Stay tuned. BREAKING: Sirens just went off at US bases in Kuwait.

“ONE ROUND. 70 FEET IN THE PITCH DARK. UNDER HEAVY RIFLE FIRE.” — Engaging an active long rifle from behind cover across 23 yards in total darkness using only a standard duty handgun is nearly impossible under live-fire stress. Wounded in the leg by an AR-15 ambush that took the lives of his two partners, Officer Alec Iurato stabilized his breathing, used a patrol cruiser as a shooting platform, and fired the single 9mm shot that ended the gunfight.

“Officer Iurato was confronted with an active, heavily armed shooter who had already killed two police officers and fired more than 80 rounds from an assault rifle. Despite suffering a severe gunshot wound to his leg, Officer Iurato took cover, evaluated the threat, and fired a single precision shot from approximately 70 feet away that neutralized the gunman. His actions were justified, heroic, and saved countless lives.”

 The 70-Foot Shot
The Coordinated Ambush: On October 12, 2022, three officers from the Bristol Police Department responded to a staged 911 call on Redstone Hill Road. As they approached, a gunman concealed in the darkness ambushed them with a semi-automatic AR-15 rifle, firing over 80 rounds of high-velocity ammunition in seconds.

Sergeant Dustin DeMonte and Officer Alex Hamzy were mortally wounded in the initial volley. Both heroes were posthumously promoted to Lieutenant and Sergeant for their ultimate sacrifice protecting the Bristol community.

Officer Iurato sustained a devastating gunshot wound when a rifle round struck his lower leg. Refusing to freeze in the kill zone, he crawled through the dark toward a parked cruiser, placing an engine block and tire between himself and the incoming rounds.

 Body-worn camera audio captures Iurato methodically regulating his respirations while rifle rounds ricocheted off the street. Staging his handgun over the cruiser’s rear quarter panel, he acquired his sights in the darkness, tracked the gunman at roughly 70 feet (23 yards), and broke a single 9mm trigger press directly into the shooter’s head, ending the ambush instantly.

The Fallacy of Handgun Limitations: Standard tactical doctrine often considers handguns effective only within 7 to 15 yards under combat stress. Iurato proved that solid fundamentals—grip, sight picture, and trigger discipline can make a standard service pistol lethal at extended rifle ranges.

Controlling the Stress Inoculation Curve: High-stress gunfights induce intense adrenaline dumps, tunnel vision, and auditory exclusion. Controlling breath tempo under cover resets heart rate just enough to execute precision motor skills.

Exploiting Improvised Hard Cover: Vehicles offer limited ballistic protection from high-velocity rifle fire, but the wheels, axles, and engine block provide substantial cover and a rigid shooting rest for stabilizing long-range pistol fire.

April 24, 2012 Dallas, TX, Army Spc. Philip C.S. Schiller, was laid to rest with full Military Honors at the DFW National Cemetery.

He was a 2010 graduate of The Colony High School — died April 11, 2012 in Kandahar province, Afghanistan, while defending his unit despite his own mortal chest wound.

Bronze Star Medal Relatives of troop members who were in the battle told his family that Spc. Schiller continued to provide machine gun cover for his unit during an enemy attack. He received the Bronze Star and the Purple Heart for his actions.

Spc. Schiller was born in Hartford, Conn., and grew up in nearby Barkhamsted. In 2009 he moved to The Colony to live with his sister, Courtney Schiller. "My brother was a fun-loving person and wanted to always help everyone in every way he could," his sister was quoted in a local paper, and said. "He was my best friend."

She talked to her brother by telephone six days before he was killed.

He had visited North Texas last month, before his deployment.

During his senior year at The Colony High School, Spc. Schiller participated in JROTC. Spc. Schiller enlisted a few weeks after he graduated from high school and completed basic training at Fort Benning, Ga., in August 2010. He was assigned to the Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Wash., that fall and was deployed to Afghanistan in March 2012.

He joined the Army ... because he wanted to be a police officer when he got out. That was his dream," his sister said.

In addition to his sister, Spc. Schiller is survived by his mother, Robin Larsen of Dallas; his father, Erik Schiller of Winsted, Conn.; and three grandparents.
Firefighters Respond to Reports of Fire at CIA Headquarters in Langley, Virginia

A U.S. Army officer arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred into U.S. military custody, British and American officials confirmed Tuesday.

U.S. officials identified the suspect as Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, a senior human resources officer stationed at Imjin Barracks — headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire. He was arrested Nov. 10 during a joint sting involving London's Counter Terrorism Policing Unit, the U.S. military, and the FBI under the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023.

U.S. authorities are continuing the investigation and say charges are expected soon, while the Kremlin has denied any involvement.

From the sidelines of Lincoln Financial Field to the front lines of Afghanistan — Rachel Washburn's story is built different.

She cheered for the Philadelphia Eagles from 2007 to 2010 while attending Drexel University on an Army ROTC scholarship, then became one of the first women selected to train and deploy with Special Operations as a Cultural Support Team (CST) member. She spent nine months embedded with Special Forces in southern Afghanistan — training local security forces, conducting over 100 combat operations, and even helping deliver a baby during a snowstorm — before returning for a second tour as an intelligence platoon leader and earning the Bronze Star Medal and Combat Action Badge.

Now Vice President of Geopolitical Intelligence & Capital Markets at veteran-owned Academy Securities, Washburn is the Eagles' 2026 Salute to Service Award nominee — and the only female veteran among all 32 team nominees this year.

With the USS Theodore Roosevelt joining the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington in CENTCOM, America hasn't concentrated this much naval firepower in the region since April.

The buildup comes as Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi warned that Tehran "will not wait for the US to attack first" — accusing Washington of using diplomacy to buy time for a new operation.

Six days. Six major system failures. And now the NSA's classified internal network is down.

According to CNN, NSA Net — the highly classified communications system used inside the National Security Agency — went offline today, forcing staggered staff arrivals while backup networks stay online. Look at the week we've had

Nov. 11–12 — Microsoft 365
Nov. 13 — FAA Air Route Traffic Control Centers
Nov. 15 — Amazon Web Services (AWS)
Nov. 16 — Major U.S. banks including Chase
Nov. 16 — United Airlines
Nov. 17 — NSA Net

Officials and companies say there's no evidence of a cyberattack behind the NSA, FAA, or Microsoft outages so far, blaming software bugs and an Arkansas router — still, six major crashes in six days has everyone side-eyeing the timeline.

Bad luck with aging tech, or something we're not being told?

#NSA #CyberSecurity #FAA

Sergeant Julia Bringloe hung beneath a helicopter on a hoist numerous times, rescuing wounded Americans. She served as a flight medic with a crew responsible for medical evacuations in Afghanistan. Over a 3 day period in 2011, Bringloe was lowered again and again into enemy fire over treacherous mountain terrain. On the first day, she dropped 150 feet to a rooftop and put a wounded soldier in a litter to be hoisted up. As the helicopter pulled them skyward, they veered towards a tree. Bringloe slammed into the tree, causing a small fracture in her leg. She ignored this to continue her mission. On another occasion, Bringloe's chopper flew into an area to rescue 3 wounded soldiers immediately after another Dustoff was shot out and had to make an emergency landing back at base. Bringloe braved the enemy fire dangling beneath the chopper once more to hoist all 3 casualties to safety. One of the soldiers was shot in the face and survived as a direct result of Bringloe's rescue and medical treatment while en route to the medical facility. For her dedication to her mission and heroic actions, Bringloe was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross.

Microsoft, the FAA, AWS, major U.S. banks, United Airlines, NSA Net, and now Apple — all inside one week.

Are your Apple services working right now, or are you getting signed out too?

How does someone work 40 years for $900 a month while a brand-new arrival gets $1,500 a month?

That's the question Marco Rubio put straight to the U.S. Senate in a 2024 floor speech that's blowing up online again. Rubio pointed to South Florida seniors who paid into Social Security for over four decades — only to watch recent arrivals qualify for $1,500 a month in refugee cash aid, Medicaid, and food stamps.

"That's real. That happens. That's happening every day. That makes no sense," Rubio said.

81 years after it was shut down, the name of America’s legendary WWII spy and commando agency is back at the Pentagon.

In a November 2 memo, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed that the Pentagon’s special operations civilian office take on the historic title: Office of Strategic Services.

It’s more than just a name change.
The move is part of an effort to elevate the role, give it more staff, more funding, and higher standing inside the Department of Defense — treating special operations more like a full military service.

Congress still has to make the biggest pieces permanent.

Big move… or just a name?

U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel Kathryn Van Auken and Major Lauralee Flannery were awarded the Bronze Star with "V" for valor for their sustained courage and heroic performance of duties while serving in Operation Iraqi Freedom.

Van Auken and Flannery had been serving together in Iraq in support of a Kuwait Exploitation Team's objective to secure, safeguard, and assist a Kuwait forensic team in the recovery of the remains of Kuwaiti Prisoners of War and Missing from the end of the 1991 Gulf War. 

Van Auken and Flannery were traveling together in the lead vehicle on February 14, 2007. They had been tasked with escorting the Kuwait Forensic Team's convoy of 12 vehicles.

It was approximately 7:30 a.m. when the middle four vehicles of the convoy were hit with the largest planned improvised explosive device (IED) attack that had been recorded up until that time. 

Ten daisy-chained 155mm mortar rounds had been buried under the raised causeway they were traveling on south of Razzazah Lake in the vicinity of Karbala, Iraq. 

When these IEDs exploded, three vehicles were destroyed, and passengers -- disoriented and bleeding -- began exiting their vehicles. 

We both exited our vehicle," Van Auken said. "[MAJ Flannery] headed east and I headed west trying to gather up everyone and secure both ends of the roadway against secondary attacks."

As team leader, Van Auken deployed rapidly, undertaking a multiplicity of actions, quickly radioing instructions to move all vehicles through the smoke and debris and to follow her vehicle into safety away from the IED site to avoid secondary devices. 

In this highly fluid situation, vehicles became disabled. Van Auken and Flannery quickly ordered the destroyed vehicles to be pushed out of the kill zone by follow-on vehicles in the convoy in order to assemble the team and get everyone to a safe and secure distance. 

Van Auken then maneuvered the front column of Polish security elements and Korean Engineer vehicles into security postures along the west side of the raised causeway with great speed and determination gaining the advantage against any follow-on IED or possible ambush. 

Both soldiers reacted fearlessly and without hesitation, running alone down the west end of the roadway to halt any oncoming traffic, orienting Iraqi vehicles to block the road, dismissing large crowds gathering, and re-positioning Polish security forces to assist. 

The team provided medical assistance to their Kuwaiti team members who had been badly cut with glass and debris and who were vomiting and shaking on the side of the road from the shocking experience. 

Their actions provided an example of urgency and purpose to fellow coalition forces, and their courage under fire unquestionably saved the lives of coalition forces, particularly the civilians in their charge.

" We are battle buddies to the end," Van Auken said.

Information and Photo and information courtesy of US Army / Dept. of Defense

HOME OF RECORD: Stow, Ohio
AWARDS BY DATE OF ACTION: Distinguished Service Cross
AWARDED FOR ACTIONS
DURING Global War on Terror
Service: Army
Battalion: 1st Battalion

CITATION:
The President of the United States of America, authorized by Act of Congress July 9, 1918, takes pleasure in presenting the Distinguished Service Cross to Sergeant Craig David Warfle, United States Army, for extraordinary heroism in connection with military operations against an armed enemy from August 18 to 19, 2010 during combat operations against an armed enemy of the United States as an Automatic Rifleman for a Joint Task Force in support of Operation Enduring Freedom. During this period, Specialist Warfle, with total disregard for his own personal safety, maneuvered on a fortified enemy machine gun position through effective enemy fire. Even after being wounded, Specialist Warfle continued to suppress the enemy with high volumes of effective fire in order to allow his team members to pull his unconscious element leader to safety. Specialist Warfle refused to be medically evacuated from the fight and his actions allowed the Platoon to hastily withdraw and defeat the enemy utilizing air assets. Specialist Warfle's distinctive accomplishments are in keeping with the finest traditions of military service and reflect great credit upon himself, this Command, and the United States Army. NARRATIVE TO ACCOMPANY AWARD: Specialist Craig D. Warfle distinguished himself by exceptionally valorous achievement as a Ranger Squad Automatic Weapons Gunner on August 18, 2010 while deployed to Afghanistan in support of Operation Enduring Freedom. Specialist Warfle was assigned to a task force, whose mission was to capture or kill Al Qaeda (AQ) and Taliban (TB) Senior Leadership. Specialist Warfle's valorous actions under effective fire while executing an objective saved the lives of his teammates and were instrumental in the death of at least 16 Taliban fighters, the removal of two Taliban Provincial Commanders, and the recovery of a large cache of weapons intended for use against Coalition Forces. On August 18, 2010, the team received special intelligence indicating that a Taliban Commander and weapons facilitator, was meeting near a tree line with at least 17 other Taliban fighters. Information gathered indicated that the enemy was orchestrating an ambush on Coalition Forces in Logar Province, Afghanistan. The team observed the fighters in position for the attack to include multiple spotters and runners used to communicate between the various fighting locations. The Battle Space Owner was notified of the imminent threat and diverted all convoys. When the enemy fighters aborted their attack they were observed walking in a military formation back towards a meeting site along a tree line. En route to that location the enemy fighters were positively identified to be carrying weapons. The team initiated a kinetic strike on the fighter's location from two AH-64s. The team stood ready and boarded two CH-47 helicopters for insertion once the kinetic strike was complete. Immediately after the kinetic strike, the team inserted a Ranger Element onto the hot landing zone to the West of the target area to eliminate the several remaining enemy combatants. Ranger Element 1, consisting of Specialist Warfle and five others, were tasked with isolating the Northern side of the tree line and suppressing the enemy to allow Ranger Element 2 to assault from West to East. Upon infiltration the Ranger Assault Force received effective enemy fire in vicinity of the North-South running tree line where the AH-64s had just completed gun runs. As soon as Specialist Warfle stepped off the ramp he came under fire from multiple enemy positions and without hesitation returned fire and crawled 15 meters through the muddy field towards the enemy. From this position, Specialist Warfle suppressed the multiple enemy positions with 150 rounds from his MK-46 allowing Ranger Element 1 to move to the North and Ranger Element 2 to maneuver to the South. Under fire and with no cover in the open field, Specialist Warfle continued to suppress the enemy positions permitting members of the Assault Force to get down in the prone position while the leaders determined a way to assault the enemy positions. After a couple of minutes passed, Ranger Element 2 came under heavy effective fire from enemy crew served weapons. Realizing that Ranger Element 2 was effectively pinned down in the open field to the South, Specialist Warfle moved with Sergeant Lugo to the North to flank the enemy position from the North-West. Specialist Warfle, while under heavy effective enemy fire, advanced on the enemy position to suppress the enemy and allow the Assault Force to maneuver on and destroy the entrenched enemy. As Sergeant Lugo and Specialist Warfle voluntarily maneuvered towards the enemy positions they identified two entrenched enemy personnel with automatic weapons firing on the Assault Force. Specialist Warfle continued to advance on the entrenched enemy using suppressive fire alone to protect Sergeant Lugo and himself because there was no available cover in open terrain. When Sergeant Lugo and Specialist Warfle got within 25 meters of the enemy machine gun positions, Specialist Warfle and Sergeant Lugo were both hit with a volley of machine gun fire. Although Specialist Warfle knew he had been shot in the right shoulder he disregarded his own personal safety and moved through the kill zone to Sergeant Lugo's side to protect his incapacitated Squad Leader. Specialist Warfle purposefully positioned himself in the line of enemy fire and immediately suppressed the enemy in order to defend Sergeant Lugo and provide covering fire for the platoon medic, Sergeant Solomon, to move to and treat Sergeant Lugo. Specialist Warfle fearlessly continued to provide accurate suppressive fire from his exposed position, allowing Staff Sergeant Myers and Sergeant Kochli the ability to move forward, suppress the enemy, and then subsequently evacuate Sergeant Lugo. Specialist Warfle continued to provide suppressive fire as Sergeant Solomon, Staff Sergeant Tucker, and Sergeant Kochli pulled Sergeant Lugo back to cover. Only after the casualty evacuation aircraft evacuated Sergeant Lugo, did Specialist Warfle treat the through and through gunshot wound to his right shoulder by applying a tourniquet to his right arm. Specialist Warfle then proceeded to engage the enemy position from a position between the enemy and the Platoon for over twenty minutes while the Assault Force reconsolidated and moved back away from the enemy positions. He steadfastly remained at his forward position delivering accurate fire on the enemy until all members of the Assault Force had moved across the open field to cover 100 meters to the West. Specialist Warfle bounded back to the West over the open field while the Assault Force provided suppressive fire. Specialist Warfle's actions allowed the Assault Force to break contact, drop ordnance on the enemy positions, and safely move to the exfiltration hot landing zone. By repeatedly risking his life for others, Specialist Warfle's purposeful gallant actions, selfless dedication to the safety of his teammates, and demonstrated extraordinary heroism were distinctive and exemplary. He is most deserving of the distinct recognition. Through his distinctive accomplishments, Specialist Warfle's personal actions reflect great credit upon himself, his unit, and the United States Army.

No sterile shoot houses. No computer simulations. Just real-world concrete, steel, and elevation pushed to the absolute limit.

DEVGRU. Always evolving.

Fair winds and following seas to Freeman Johnson — the oldest surviving Pearl Harbor veteran, who passed away Saturday at age 106 in Centerville, Massachusetts.

His ship evaded midget submarines and fought its way out to open sea, and Johnson went on to witness Japan's surrender in Tokyo Bay from the USS Iowa in 1945.

Asked about his service years later, he stayed humble — saying, "I wasn't brave, I was there. I just did what I was told. I did my job." After the Navy, he married his wife Ruth, raised three daughters, served as a foster parent, worked 40 years in a machine shop, and didn't retire until 90.

Surrounded and severely outnumbered in combat, you can either give up or fight to the death. Petty Officer Luttrell and three other SEALs faced that decision in the hills of Afghanistan on June 28, 2005. A SEAL never gives up!

The team, which included Lt. Michael Murphy and Petty Officers Matt Axelson and Danny Dietz, had been sent on a covert mission to find and kill a Taliban leader. As the SEALs scoured the area, they encountered three civilians who Luttrell believes alerted Taliban fighters. About an hour later, approximately 80-100 Taliban fighters appeared and began a ferocious assault. As the small team fought back, a Chinook helicopter arrived in support – but was shot down by the enemy, killing all 16 men on board.

The SEALs realized that their odds of survival were slim – but their training and sense of honor told them to take out as many enemies as they could. By the end of a two-hour gunfight that careened through the hills and over cliffs, Murphy, Axelson, and Dietz had fallen.

An estimated 35 Taliban were also dead. Luttrell managed to escape the carnage – badly injured – and slowly crawl away down the side of a cliff.

Dehydrated, with a bullet wound to one leg, shrapnel embedded in both legs, three vertebrae cracked; the situation for Luttrell was grim. Rescue helicopters were sent in, but he was too weak and injured to make contact. Traveling seven miles on foot, he eventually reached a village where he was put under “lokhay warkawal,” Afghan for the protection of the villagers, who fed him and cleaned his wounds. In short order, one of the villagers made his way to a Marine outpost with a note from Luttrell, and U.S. forces launched a massive rescue operation that pulled him from enemy territory. To this day, Luttrell remains indebted to the villagers who risked their lives in his defense. “THEIR HELICOPTER WAS SHOT DOWN: HE LED THE TEAM RIGHT BACK UP THE MOUNTAIN.”

In the early morning hours of March 4, 2002, atop the freezing, 10,000-foot peak of Takur Ghar in eastern Afghanistan, seven American warriors fought one of the most ferocious, desperate close-quarters battles of Operation Anaconda.

Serving as the team leader of a joint reconnaissance element (Mako 30), Senior Chief Petty Officer Britt K. Slabinski and his Navy SEALs were attempting an insertion when their MH-47E Chinook was ambushed by concealed al-Qaeda fighters firing RPGs and heavy machine guns.

During the evasive maneuvers, Petty Officer First Class Neil Roberts was thrown from the rear ramp into the deep snow. The severely damaged helicopter crash-landed miles away in the valley below.

Knowing Roberts was stranded alone surrounded by an entrenched enemy force, Slabinski didn’t wait for a conventional quick-reaction force. He rallied his five remaining teammates, boarded a second Chinook, and ordered the pilots to fly right back into the teeth of the enemy ambush atop the peak.

What unfolded on that ridge defined the unyielding ethos of the Special Operations community:

Stepping off the helicopter into waist-deep snow and freezing blizzards, the team was instantly met by a barrage of interlocking machine-gun and sniper fire from reinforced bunkers just meters away.

 Slabinski led the charge through the snow, repeatedly exposing himself to direct fire and grenade blasts to engage the bunkers, clear enemy fighting positions, and protect wounded teammates.

Trapped on an open, snow-covered precipice and low on ammunition, Slabinski coordinated precision airstrikes within danger-close range of his own position to prevent the enemy from overrunning their line.

14 Hours on the High Ground: Maneuvering his wounded men to a defensible position under relentless fire, Slabinski directed the medical defense and sustained the perimeter for 14 grueling hours until extraction was secured.

On May 24, 2018, President Donald J. Trump presented Master Chief Britt K. Slabinski with the Medal of Honor at the White House, recognizing his extraordinary valor and refusal to leave a fallen brother behind.

A bond forged in the fires of combat that outlasted the battlefield and saved two lives.

Former DEVGRU (SEAL Team 6) operator Will "Cheese" Chesney seated inside a transport helicopter beside his legendary four-legged teammate, Cairo—the only military working dog on the raid that took down Osama bin Laden.

Pairing up in 2008, Chesney and the Belgian Malinois were virtually inseparable, running hundreds of high-threat direct-action raids across the Global War on Terror. In 2009, Cairo took bullet fire while chasing down enemy insurgents, dragging himself back to Chesney, who fought desperately to keep him alive. Two years later, on the historic night of May 2, 2011, Cairo sat between Chesney’s boots inside a stealth Black Hawk heading into Abbottabad for Operation Neptune Spear—kitted with a Kevlar vest and night vision to secure the perimeter and screen for explosives. In the aftermath of the raid, Cairo was the only operational name released to the public.

The war took a heavy toll on both of them. In 2013, a grenade blast left Chesney with a severe traumatic brain injury and PTSD. As conventional medical treatments failed to break through the crippling migraines and depression, visiting a retired Cairo proved to be his lifeline. Chesney successfully adopted him, allowing the two warriors to nurse each other's scars through Cairo’s final years until cancer claimed the dog in 2015.

Immortalized in Chesney’s memoir No Ordinary Dog, their story stands as the ultimate testament to loyalty between handler and K9.

A man, his dog, and an eternal brotherhood.

Rest in peace, Cairo. The Only Easy Day Was Yesterday. 🇺🇸🔱🐾⚡🦅
